chapter.name: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life

questions.q: Farmers beat bundles of harvested wheat stalks on a large wooden log so that the grains come off the stalks. What is this process called?
questions.a: Threshing
o: Threshing
Winnowing
Handpicking
Sieving

questions.q: While eating upma, Rohan notices a few curry leaves in it. He takes them out one by one with his fingers and keeps them on the side of his plate. Which method of separation is he using?
questions.a: Handpicking
o: Handpicking
Threshing
Winnowing
Decantation

questions.q:
Match each task in Column I with what it is called in Column II.
Column I: 1. Taking whole black peppers out of pulao and keeping them aside on the plate  2. Beating bundles of dried ragi stalks with a stick so that the grains fall off  3. Tipping threshed ragi from a soop in front of a table fan in a closed room  4. A machine that takes harvested stalks and gives out grain free of both stalks and husk
Column II: A. Winnowing  B. Thresher  C. Handpicking  D. Threshing

Assertion (A): Handpicking is not a convenient way to remove the husk from a big heap of threshed wheat.
Reason (R): Handpicking is done on the basis of differences in size, colour and shape of the particles.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is handpicking? (b) Give one example of handpicking from your kitchen.
questions.a: (a) Handpicking is the method of picking out particles by hand from a mixture, on the basis of differences in size, colour and shape of the particles. (b) Any one, for example: picking small stones out of rice or pulses before cooking, or taking whole black peppers out of pulao.
s: (a) Picking particles out of a mixture by hand, using differences in size, colour or shape
(b) Gives one correct kitchen example such as removing stones from rice or pulses

questions.q: True or False: 'In winnowing, the wind blows the grains away and the husk falls close to the farmer.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The husk is lighter, so the wind or blowing air carries it away; the heavier grains fall close to the farmer.
s: States False
Corrects it: the lighter husk is blown away and the heavier grains fall close by

questions.q: Gopal wants clean wheat grain from bundles of freshly harvested, dried wheat stalks. He decides not to beat the stalks and to winnow the bundles straight away in a strong wind. (a) Why will winnowing not give him loose grain? (b) What must be done first, and what does it do?
questions.a: (a) The grains are still attached to the stalks. Winnowing only separates loose, lighter husk from loose, heavier grains; the wind cannot pull the grains off the stalks. (b) Threshing: the stalks are beaten (for example on a wooden log) to separate the grains from them. The loose grain, mixed with husk, can then be winnowed.
s: (a) The grains are still on the stalks; winnowing only separates loose husk from loose grain
(b) Threshing first: beating the stalks separates the grains from them, then winnowing removes the husk

questions.q: Answer these about winnowing. (a) Name the bamboo tray traditionally used for winnowing. (b) Which component falls closer to the farmer during winnowing: the grains or the husk? (c) Name the machine that does both threshing and winnowing at the same time.
questions.a: (a) A soop. (b) The grains, because they are heavier. (c) A thresher (threshing machine).
s: (a) Names the soop (bamboo tray)
(b) The heavier grains fall closer
(c) Names the thresher

questions.q:
After the jowar harvest in a village near Nashik, Kamala's family spreads the cut stalks in the sun to dry. Next they beat the stalks on a wooden log, and the loose grain falls in a heap mixed with a lot of husk. On Monday a steady wind blows, but on Tuesday the air is completely still. After cleaning, a 50 kg sack of grain is found to have about 10 small stones in it.
(a) Name the process of beating the stalks on the log.
(b) Which method should the family use on Monday to remove the husk, and what does it depend on?
(c) Why will this method not work well outdoors on Tuesday, and what could they use instead of wind?
(d) Which method should remove the 10 stones from the sack, and why does it suit this case?
questions.a: (a) Threshing. (b) Winnowing, using a soop in the wind; it depends on the husk being lighter than the grain, so the wind carries the husk away while the heavier grain falls close by. (c) There is no wind on Tuesday to carry the husk away; they can blow air, for example with a fan. (d) Handpicking, because the stones are few in number and can easily be picked out by hand.
s: (a) Names threshing
(b) Names winnowing and says lighter husk is carried by wind while heavier grain falls near
(c) No wind to carry the husk; uses blown air such as a fan instead
(d) Handpicking, because the stones are few and easy to pick

questions.q:
A 40 kg heap on a threshing floor holds 30 kg of rice grains, 9.6 kg of husk and 0.4 kg of small stones (about 200 stones, each much heavier than a rice grain). Javed has a soop, a windy afternoon and two helpers.
(a) Which method should he use first on the whole heap, and why?
(b) If the wind carries away all of the husk and nothing else, what mass is left in the heap near his feet?
(c) Will winnowing remove the stones? Give a reason.
(d) Which method should he use next for the stones, and on what differences does it depend?
(e) His helper says, 'Let us pick out the stones first and winnow later.' Judge this order.
questions.a: (a) Winnowing, because the husk is a large, light component that the wind can carry away, while the grains are heavier and fall near him. (b) 30 kg + 0.4 kg = 30.4 kg. (c) No. The stones are heavy, like the grains, so they are not blown away; they fall near his feet with the grains. (d) Handpicking, which works on differences in size, colour and shape; it is convenient now because the stones are few and the husk has gone. (e) It is a poor order: with 9.6 kg of husk still mixed in, the 200 stones are hard to see and pick, so it wastes time. Winnowing first, then handpicking, is better.
s: (a) Chooses winnowing first because the husk is lighter and present in a large amount
(b) Finds 30.4 kg left near his feet
(c) Says the heavy stones are not blown away and stay with the grain
(d) Handpicking, using differences in size, colour and shape
(e) Rejects the order: picking stones out of a husky heap is slow; winnow first, then handpick

questions.q: Sieving is used to separate the components of a solid-solid mixture when the components differ in which property?
questions.a: The size of their particles
o: The size of their particles
The colour of their particles
Whether they are attracted to a magnet
Whether they dissolve in water

questions.q: Four mixtures are kept on a kitchen counter. Which one can be separated by passing it through a sieve?
questions.a: Wheat flour with bran in it
o: Wheat flour with bran in it
Common salt dissolved in water
Rice flour stirred into water
Sugar and salt crystals of the same size

questions.q: A mixture contains whole green moong (about 4 mm across), poppy seeds (about 1 mm) and fine dust (about 0.1 mm). Shabnam has sieves with holes of 0.05 mm, 0.5 mm, 2 mm and 6 mm. She will shake the mixture through one sieve and then shake whatever passes through it on a second sieve. Which pair, in this order, gives all three parts separately?
questions.a: The 2 mm sieve first, then the 0.5 mm sieve
o: The 2 mm sieve first, then the 0.5 mm sieve
The 6 mm sieve first, then the 2 mm sieve
The 0.5 mm sieve first, then the 0.05 mm sieve
The 2 mm sieve first, then the 6 mm sieve

questions.q:
Read the statements about sieving.
I. Sieves are used at construction sites to separate pebbles and stones from sand.
II. Sieving will still separate two solids if the holes of the sieve are larger than the particles of both.
III. When flour is sieved, the fine flour particles pass through the holes of the sieve.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III only
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Small stones in wheat flour stay on top of the sieve when the flour is sieved.
Reason (R): The small stones are bigger than the holes of the sieve, while the fine flour particles are smaller than the holes.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) When is sieving used to separate a mixture? (b) Give one example of sieving used outside the kitchen.
questions.a: (a) Sieving is used when the components of a solid-solid mixture have different sizes. (b) At construction sites, sieves separate pebbles and stones from sand.
s: (a) States that sieving is used for a solid-solid mixture whose components differ in size
(b) Gives an example such as separating pebbles and stones from sand at a construction site

questions.q: Ayaan has one sieve with holes about 3 mm wide. Will it separate (a) ajwain seeds (about 2 mm) from whole chickpeas (about 8 mm)? (b) ajwain seeds from cumin seeds of nearly the same size? Give a reason for each.
questions.a: (a) Yes. The ajwain seeds are smaller than the holes and pass through, while the chickpeas are bigger than the holes and stay on the sieve. (b) No. Both kinds of seeds are of nearly the same size, so both pass through the holes together; sieving needs a difference in size.
s: (a) Yes: ajwain passes through the 3 mm holes while the larger chickpeas stay on top
(b) No: seeds of the same size pass through together, so sieving cannot separate them

questions.q: Pooja says, 'A sieve with bigger holes lets the flour through faster, so the sieve with the biggest holes is always the best one for removing bran from flour.' Check her claim and give your verdict with reasons.
questions.a: She is only partly right. A sieve with bigger holes does let flour through faster. But if the holes are larger than the bran flakes and small stones, these also pass through with the flour and nothing is separated. The best sieve has holes smaller than the bran and stones but bigger than the fine flour particles.
s: Agrees that bigger holes let the flour pass faster
Explains that holes larger than the bran and stones let them pass too, so no separation happens
Concludes partly right: the holes must be smaller than the bran but bigger than the flour particles

questions.q: At a spice mill in Guntur, 10 kg of dry red chillies is ground once. The ground material holds 6 kg of fine powder (particles under 0.3 mm) and 4 kg of coarse flakes and seed bits (1 to 4 mm). Only the fine powder is packed for sale. The miller has two sieves, one with 0.5 mm holes and one with 5 mm holes. (a) Which sieve should he use, and why? (b) What mass passes through that sieve, and what mass stays on it? (c) He grinds what stayed on the sieve a second time, which turns three-quarters of it into fine powder, and sieves it again. How much more powder does he get, and what mass still stays on the sieve? (d) What total mass of powder can he pack from the 10 kg of chillies, and what fraction of the chillies is this?
questions.a: (a) The 0.5 mm sieve: the powder (under 0.3 mm) is smaller than its holes and passes, while the flakes and seed bits (1 mm or more) are bigger and stay on it. The 5 mm sieve would let both through. (b) 6 kg passes; 4 kg stays on the sieve. (c) Three-quarters of 4 kg = 3 kg more powder; 4 - 3 = 1 kg still stays on the sieve. (d) 6 + 3 = 9 kg, which is 9/10 of the 10 kg of chillies.
s: (a) Chooses the 0.5 mm sieve: powder is smaller than the holes, flakes and seed bits are bigger
(b) 6 kg passes and 4 kg stays
(c) 3 kg more powder after regrinding; 1 kg still stays
(d) 9 kg in all, which is 9/10 of the chillies

questions.q: Mami sieves wheat flour before making meethi puris. (a) Name two things that stay on the sieve. (b) What passes through the holes of the sieve? (c) Why does she sieve the flour before kneading it? (d) A tin of rice flour has a few broken rice grains in it. When it is shaken on a fine sieve, what stays on the sieve? (e) A sieve has 1 mm holes. A mixture holds particles about 0.2 mm across and particles about 3 mm across. Which particles stay on the sieve?
questions.a: (a) Bran and small stones. (b) The fine flour particles. (c) To remove the bran (and small stones) from the flour, because these are not wanted in the dish; the flour must be cleaned of them before a dish is prepared. (d) The broken rice grains, because they are bigger than the holes, while the fine rice flour passes through. (e) The 3 mm particles stay on the sieve; the 0.2 mm particles pass through.
s: (a) Names bran and small stones
(b) Fine flour passes through
(c) To remove the unwanted bran (and stones) before preparing the dish
(d) The broken rice grains stay on the sieve
(e) The 3 mm particles stay on the 1 mm sieve

questions.q: What is evaporation?
questions.a: The process in which a liquid gets converted into its vapour
o: The process in which a liquid gets converted into its vapour
The process in which water vapour changes into its liquid state
The settling of a heavier insoluble solid at the bottom of a liquid
The passing of a liquid through a material with fine pores

questions.q: How is salt obtained from seawater?
questions.a: The seawater is kept in shallow pits open to sunlight and air until the water evaporates.
o: The seawater is kept in shallow pits open to sunlight and air until the water evaporates.
The seawater is poured through fine filter paper so that all the salt stays behind on it as residue.
The seawater is left standing in deep tanks so that the salt settles and the water above is poured off.
The seawater is churned for a long time so that the salt floats to the top and can be skimmed off.

questions.q: Lata stirs two spoons of sugar into a glass of water until no sugar can be seen. She now wants the sugar back as a solid. Which method will work?
questions.a: Evaporating the water from the solution
o: Evaporating the water from the solution
Filtering the solution through filter paper
Letting it stand and then decanting the water
Pouring the solution through a fine sieve

questions.q:
Match each everyday situation in Column I with the process it shows in Column II.
Column I: 1. A puddle of salty water on a steel plate in the sun leaves a white crust  2. Tea is gently poured into a cup after the tea leaves have settled  3. Pond water passes through a cotton plug in a funnel and comes out clearer  4. Lumps are removed from besan by shaking it through a mesh
Column II: A. Sieving  B. Filtration  C. Decantation  D. Evaporation
True or False: 'When a salt solution is heated in a china dish until all the water boils away, the salt is left behind in the dish.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Heating turns the water into vapour, which leaves the dish, but the dissolved salt does not go with it; once the dish cools, the salt can be felt in it.
s: States True
Reason: the water changes into vapour and escapes, while the salt stays in the dish

questions.q: (a) Name one water body in India that contains common salt. (b) Name the process that removes the water when seawater is kept in shallow pits in the sun.
questions.a: (a) Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan. (b) Evaporation.
s: (a) Names Sambhar Lake (Rajasthan)
(b) Names evaporation

questions.q: Ravi spreads a few drops of salt solution on a piece of thick black paper and leaves it to dry. (a) What does he see on the paper after it dries? (b) What substance is left on the paper? (c) Where has the water gone?
questions.a: (a) White patches on the black paper. (b) Salt. (c) The water has evaporated: it has changed into vapour and gone into the air.
s: (a) White patches are seen
(b) The patches are salt
(c) The water has evaporated into the air as vapour

questions.q: A shopkeeper has accidentally dissolved 50 g of common salt in a bucket of clean water and wants the salt back. Three friends suggest: Mohan, 'Pour it through filter paper'; Sita, 'Let it stand, then pour off the water'; Imran, 'Heat it until the water boils away'. For each suggestion, say whether it will give the salt back, with a reason.
questions.a: Mohan: No. The salt is dissolved, so it passes through the filter paper with the water; filtration holds back only insoluble solid particles. Sita: No. Dissolved salt does not settle at the bottom, so sedimentation and decantation leave the salt in the water that is poured off. Imran: Yes. Heating evaporates the water and leaves the dissolved salt behind.
s: Filtration fails because dissolved salt passes through the filter paper
Sedimentation and decantation fail because dissolved salt does not settle
Evaporation works: the water leaves as vapour and the salt is left behind

questions.q:
A Class 6 group from Thoothukudi visits a salt pan on the coast. The guide fills a shallow pit with 4,000 litres of seawater. After about eight hot, breezy days the water is gone, and a white solid is left in the pit. The guide says each litre of this seawater leaves 32 g of this solid. Back at school, the group wants to show salt being made from salt solution within one 40-minute period.
(a) Name the process that removed the water from the pit.
(b) What mass of solid, in kilograms, is left in the pit?
(c) Is this solid pure common salt? Give a reason.
(d) For the class show, should the group dry salt solution in the sun or heat it in a china dish? Justify, and name one care they must take.
questions.a: (a) Evaporation. (b) 4,000 x 32 g = 1,28,000 g = 128 kg. (c) No. Seawater has several salts and some other substances dissolved in it, so a solid mixture is left; common salt is obtained from it by further purification. (d) Heating in a china dish, because in the sun the water would take far longer than one period to evaporate, while boiling it away over a flame is quick. They must be careful while heating the china dish, so the teacher should demonstrate it.
s: (a) Names evaporation
(b) Calculates 128 kg
(c) No: seawater holds other salts and substances, so the solid needs further purification
(d) Chooses heating in a china dish for speed within the period and names care while heating

questions.q:
A salt worker on the Odisha coast tests the water from two creeks before filling her salt pit. She dries 250 mL of water from creek A on a shallow plate in the sun and gets 7.5 g of white solid. She dries 400 mL of water from creek B in the same way and gets 10 g of white solid.
(a) Name the process by which the water left the plates.
(b) How many grams of solid does one litre of water from each creek leave?
(c) Which creek has the saltier water? Her friend says, 'Creek B, because its plate gave more solid.' Explain why the friend is wrong.
(d) Her pit holds 5,000 litres. How many kilograms of solid would it give if it is filled from creek A?
(e) How many litres of creek B water would she need to get the same mass of solid?
questions.a: (a) Evaporation. (b) Creek A: 7.5 g in 0.25 L = 30 g per litre. Creek B: 10 g in 0.4 L = 25 g per litre. (c) Creek A. Plate B gave more solid only because more water (400 mL) was dried on it; the amounts must be compared for the same volume, and per litre A leaves 30 g while B leaves 25 g. (d) 5,000 x 30 g = 1,50,000 g = 150 kg. (e) 1,50,000 g / 25 g per litre = 6,000 litres.
s: (a) Names evaporation
(b) 30 g per litre for A and 25 g per litre for B
(c) Chooses A: B gave more only because more water was dried; compare per litre
(d) 150 kg from 5,000 litres of creek A
(e) 6,000 litres of creek B

questions.q: What is the settling down of a heavier insoluble component at the bottom of a liquid called?
questions.a: Sedimentation
o: Sedimentation
Decantation
Filtration
Evaporation

questions.q: Muddy water is poured into a filter-paper cone placed in a funnel over a conical flask. What is the mud that stays on the filter paper called?
questions.a: Residue
o: Residue
Filtrate
Solution
Vapour

questions.q: Which of these is NOT an example of filtration?
questions.a: Pouring tea gently from a pan after the tea leaves have settled at the bottom
o: Pouring tea gently from a pan after the tea leaves have settled at the bottom
Pouring hot tea through a tea strainer so that all the tea leaves collect in it
Pouring muddy water through a filter-paper cone so that the mud stays on the paper
Pouring pond water through a clean piece of cloth so that the dirt stays on the cloth

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Decantation is used while washing rice before cooking.
Reason (R): The heavier rice grains settle at the bottom, so the water above them can be poured off by tilting the vessel.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Decantation separates every solid particle from a liquid.
II. The very small pores between the woven threads of a cloth let it act as a filter.
III. In filtration, the solid particles held back by the filter are called the residue.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III only
o: II and III only
I and II only
I and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: (a) Differentiate between the residue and the filtrate in filtration. (b) When muddy water is filtered through filter paper, name the residue and the filtrate.
questions.a: (a) The residue is the solid that is held back on the filter; the filtrate is the liquid that passes through the filter. (b) The mud is the residue and the clear water collected in the flask is the filtrate.
s: (a) Residue is the solid held back; filtrate is the liquid that passes through
(b) Mud is the residue; clear water is the filtrate

questions.q: True or False: 'Water from a village well was left to stand overnight, and the top water was then poured off carefully. Because this water looks clear, it has no solid particles left in it.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Decantation does not completely separate all the solid particles from a liquid; some fine particles can still be carried along with the water that is poured off. Filtering it through a filter with very fine pores, such as filter paper, removes more of them.
s: States False
Reason: decantation does not remove all particles; fine particles may remain, and filtration removes more

questions.q: In a class activity, Arif folds a filter paper into a cone, but he tears a small hole at its tip. He places the cone in a funnel over a conical flask and pours muddy water into it. (a) What will the liquid collected in the flask look like? Give a reason. (b) His partner places a fresh, untorn filter-paper cone in the funnel and pours this liquid through it again. What will the liquid in the flask look like now, and why? (c) In (b), what is the residue and what is the filtrate?
questions.a: (a) Still muddy. The hole is much bigger than the mud particles, so the muddy water runs through the hole without being filtered. (b) Clear. The untorn filter paper has very fine pores; water passes through them, but the mud particles are too big to pass and are held back. (c) The mud left on the filter paper is the residue; the clear water collected in the flask is the filtrate.
s: (a) Still muddy, because mud passes through the hole, which is larger than the mud particles
(b) Clear, because the fine pores of untorn filter paper let water through but hold back the mud
(c) Mud on the paper is the residue; clear water in the flask is the filtrate

questions.q: A hostel kitchen in Guwahati receives a drum of cloudy water that has sand and fine mud in it. The cook has a clean bucket, a funnel and filter paper. Describe, step by step, how to get clear water using sedimentation, decantation and filtration, in that order. For each step, say what is done and what happens. Also explain why the cook must not shake or stir the drum just before pouring.
questions.a: Step 1, sedimentation: leave the water undisturbed for some time so that the heavier sand and mud settle at the bottom. Step 2, decantation: tilt the drum gently and pour the water on top into the clean bucket, leaving the settled layer behind. Step 3, filtration: pour the decanted water through filter paper in the funnel; the mud stays on the paper as residue and clear water passes as filtrate. The drum must not be shaken or stirred, because that would mix the settled sand and mud back into the water, and the poured water would be cloudy again.
s: Sedimentation: leaves it undisturbed so the heavier sand and mud settle
Decantation: pours off the top water by tilting, leaving the settled layer behind
Filtration through filter paper: mud as residue, clear water as filtrate
Shaking or stirring would mix the settled solid back into the water

questions.q:
In Dadi's kitchen in Ludhiana, 2 kg of homemade butter is heated slowly in a heavy pan to make ghee. When it is ready, the pan holds clear golden ghee, and small brown bits slowly sink to the bottom. Dadi leaves the pan undisturbed for 15 minutes so that it cools a little. Then she tilts it gently and pours 1,450 g of clear ghee into a steel jar, stopping when the brown bits start to move. She pours the last 230 g, a mix of ghee and brown bits, through a clean muslin cloth, and 180 g of ghee comes through.
(a) Name the process in which the brown bits collect at the bottom of the pan.
(b) Name the method Dadi uses to pour off the clear ghee, and say why she tilts the pan gently.
(c) What total mass of ghee does she collect?
(d) In the last step, what is the residue and what is the filtrate? What lets the cloth act as a filter?
questions.a: (a) Sedimentation: the heavier brown bits settle at the bottom of the liquid ghee. (b) Decantation. She tilts gently so that the settled brown bits are not disturbed and stay at the bottom while the clear ghee flows out. (c) 1,450 g + 180 g = 1,630 g. (d) The brown bits left on the muslin are the residue; the ghee that comes through is the filtrate. The cloth has very small pores between its woven threads, which let the ghee pass but hold back the bits.
s: (a) Names sedimentation
(b) Decantation; tilting gently keeps the settled bits undisturbed at the bottom
(c) Calculates 1,630 g
(d) Brown bits are the residue, ghee is the filtrate; the small pores between the threads act as the filter

questions.q: Which tool is traditionally used to churn curd to separate butter?
questions.a: A mathni (churner)
o: A mathni (churner)
A soop (bamboo tray)
A sieve
A china dish

questions.q: Four mixtures are kept on a table. In which one will moving a magnet through the mixture pull out one of the components?
questions.a: Iron screws mixed with dry peanuts
o: Iron screws mixed with dry peanuts
Common salt mixed with fine sand
Husk mixed with threshed wheat grains
Butter mixed with buttermilk after churning

questions.q:
Match each mixture in Column I with the method used to separate it in Column II.
Column I: 1. Butter from curd  2. Scrap iron from a heap of factory waste  3. Bran from wheat flour  4. Tea leaves from tea, using a strainer
Column II: A. Sieving  B. Filtration  C. Churning  D. Magnetic separation

Assertion (A): A crane magnet lifts iron scrap out of a heap of waste but leaves the plastic and glass behind.
Reason (R): Scrap iron can be recycled and reused.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is magnetic separation? (b) Give one use of magnetic separation in industry.
questions.a: (a) Magnetic separation is the separation of magnetic substances from non-magnetic substances by using a magnet. (b) In many industries, scrap iron is separated from heaps of waste material using magnets fitted to a crane, so that it can be recycled.
s: (a) Separating magnetic from non-magnetic substances using a magnet
(b) Gives a use such as crane magnets pulling scrap iron out of waste

questions.q: True or False: 'A magnet moved through a heap of sawdust that contains iron nails will pull out the nails but leave the sawdust behind.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Iron is a magnetic substance, so the nails are attracted to the magnet, while sawdust is not attracted to it.
s: States True
Reason: iron nails are magnetic and are attracted; sawdust is not

questions.q: Kunal says, 'Churning and winnowing work on the same kind of difference between the two parts of a mixture.' (a) State the difference between the components that each method uses. (b) Is Kunal right? Give one way the two methods are also different.
questions.a: (a) Both use a difference in lightness: in winnowing the lighter husk is blown away from the heavier grain; in churning the lighter butter floats to the top while the buttermilk is left behind. (b) Yes, he is right about the difference used. But they differ in how it is used: winnowing uses wind or blowing air on a dry solid mixture, while churning is done in a liquid (curd) and the butter floats.
s: (a) Both use lighter versus heavier: husk blown away; butter floats
(b) Agrees, and gives one difference such as air on a dry mixture versus floating in curd

questions.q: A dhaba owner in Bhopal churns curd in a big pot every morning. (a) Name this method of separation. (b) Which component floats to the top, and why? (c) What is left behind in the pot?
questions.a: (a) Churning. (b) Butter floats to the top because it is lighter. (c) Buttermilk (chhach).
s: (a) Names churning
(b) Butter floats because it is lighter
(c) Buttermilk is left behind

questions.q:
Sunita churns 5 litres of curd with a mathni and collects 175 g of butter in 25 minutes. Her neighbour churns the same amount of curd in an electric mixer and collects the same amount of butter in 6 minutes.
(a) Name the method of separation both of them use.
(b) Why does the butter collect at the top?
(c) How many grams of butter does each litre of curd give?
(d) Churning 5 litres at a time, how many minutes would the mixer need to give 700 g of butter?
(e) After churning, the buttermilk is also drunk. Is this separation done to get two useful components or to remove one component that is not useful? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Churning. (b) Butter is lighter, so it floats to the top while the buttermilk is left behind. (c) 175 g / 5 = 35 g per litre. (d) 700 g needs 700 / 35 = 20 litres of curd, which is 20 / 5 = 4 batches; 4 x 6 = 24 minutes. (e) To get two useful components: the butter is used, and the buttermilk (chhach) is drunk.
s: (a) Names churning
(b) Butter is lighter and floats to the top
(c) Calculates 35 g of butter per litre
(d) Finds 20 litres, that is 4 batches, so 24 minutes
(e) Two useful components, since both butter and buttermilk are used

questions.q: A cattle-feed mill near Anand finds short bits of iron wire mixed into its chopped dry fodder. To test, a worker spreads a 10 kg sample on a mat and sweeps a strong magnet through it three times. The first sweep picks up 30 wire bits, the second picks up 6 and the third picks up none. The mill prepares 600 kg of fodder every day. (a) How many wire bits were in the sample, and why does the worker stop after the third sweep? (b) If the sample is typical, about how many wire bits come in each day's fodder? (c) Why does the magnet pick up the wire bits but not the fodder? (d) The owner says, 'One sweep of each day's fodder is enough.' Judge this using the data.
questions.a: (a) 30 + 6 + 0 = 36 bits. The third sweep picked up none, so no more wire bits that the magnet can reach are left. (b) 600 kg is 60 times 10 kg, so about 36 x 60 = 2,160 bits a day. (c) Iron is a magnetic substance and is attracted to the magnet; the dry fodder is non-magnetic and is not attracted. (d) The owner is wrong. In the test, one sweep took only 30 of the 36 bits and left 6, so one sweep of 600 kg would leave about 6 x 60 = 360 bits in the fodder. The fodder should be swept again and again until a sweep picks up no more wire.
s: (a) 36 bits; stops because the third sweep found none
(b) About 2,160 bits a day
(c) Iron is magnetic and is attracted; fodder is non-magnetic
(d) Rejects one sweep: it leaves about 360 bits a day; sweep until a sweep picks up none

questions.q: Before cooking, Nisha removes small stones from a plate of toor dal. For which of the two purposes of separation is she doing this?
questions.a: To remove a component that is not useful
o: To remove a component that is not useful
To obtain two different but useful components
To separate a lighter component from a heavier one by blowing air
To get back a solid that is dissolved in a liquid

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does a mixture that has more than two components generally require?
questions.a: A combination of several methods of separation
o: A combination of several methods of separation
Only one method of separation, repeated many times
Sieving alone, using a sieve with holes of the right size
Filtration alone, because a filter holds back every solid

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. Separating iron nails, common salt and water from one another needs more than one method of separation.
II. When a mixture of sand and common salt is stirred in water and filtered, the salt is left on the filter paper.
III. Removing small stones from rice is done to obtain two different but useful components.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Black pepper and common salt that are mixed in water can both be got back separately by evaporation alone.
Reason (R): A mixture that has more than two components generally requires a combination of several methods of separation.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: State the two purposes for which we separate the substances in a mixture, and give one example of each.
questions.a: (1) To obtain two different but useful components, for example churning curd to get both butter and buttermilk. (2) To remove a component that is not useful, for example picking small stones out of pulses.
s: States 'to get two different useful components' with a fitting example such as butter and buttermilk
States 'to remove a component that is not useful' with a fitting example such as stones from pulses

questions.q: A jar holds a dry mixture of sawdust and common salt. It is stirred into water until the salt dissolves. (a) Which method now separates the sawdust, and why does it work? (b) How is the salt then recovered from what is left?
questions.a: (a) Filtration: sawdust does not dissolve, so it is held back on the filter as the residue, while the salt solution passes through as the filtrate. (b) By evaporating the water from the filtrate, for example by heating it in a china dish, which leaves the salt behind.
s: (a) Filtration, because the insoluble sawdust stays as residue and the salt solution passes
(b) Evaporates the filtrate to leave the salt behind

questions.q: Before cooking, Ravi washes a bowl of masoor dal that has some dust and a few small stones in it. He says, 'I do not need to pick out anything. When I wash the dal and pour the water off, the dust and the stones will both go out with the water.' Check his claim and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. Washing the dal and pouring off the water (decantation) does carry the dust away in the water, which is why decantation is used for washing pulses. But the small stones are heavy: they settle at the bottom with the dal and stay in the bowl when the water is poured off. They must be removed by handpicking, which is convenient because they are few and differ from the dal in colour and shape. So two methods are needed, not one.
s: Agrees that the dust is carried away in the poured-off water (decantation)
Shows that the heavy stones settle with the dal and are not poured off
Verdict partly right: the stones must be handpicked, so two methods are needed

questions.q: The sweepings from a school's woodwork room hold dry fine sand, sawdust and a few small iron nails. The sawdust bits and the sand grains are about the same size. The teacher wants the three parts separately without using any water. (a) Which part should be removed with a magnet, and why? (b) How can the sawdust then be separated from the sand, and which difference between them does this use? (c) Why would a sieve not separate the sawdust from the sand here?
questions.a: (a) The iron nails, because iron is a magnetic substance and is attracted to the magnet, while sand and sawdust are not. (b) By blowing air over the mixture, for example with a fan or in the wind, as in winnowing: the lighter sawdust is blown away and the heavier sand stays behind. This uses the difference between lighter and heavier components. (c) Sieving works only when the components differ in size; here the sawdust and sand are about the same size, so they would pass through the holes, or stay on the sieve, together.
s: (a) Iron nails, because iron is magnetic
(b) Blowing air carries away the lighter sawdust and leaves the heavier sand
(c) Sieving needs a size difference; same-size sawdust and sand behave the same on a sieve

questions.q:
In a school kitchen in Indore, a 2 kg tin of sooji (grains about 0.5 mm across) falls onto an open tray that holds 300 g of mustard seeds (about 2 mm across), and a few small iron pins from a torn packet fall in too. The cook wants the sooji and the mustard seeds back, clean and separate. She has a magnet and a sieve with 1 mm holes. Each mustard seed weighs about 5 mg.
(a) Which method should take out the pins, and why?
(b) When the rest is shaken on the 1 mm sieve, what passes through and what stays on it?
(c) About how many mustard seeds are on the tray?
(d) A helper says, 'Let us just pick the mustard seeds out by hand.' Judge this suggestion using your answer to (c).
questions.a: (a) Magnetic separation: the iron pins are attracted to the magnet because iron is a magnetic substance, while sooji and mustard seeds are not. (b) The sooji (0.5 mm) is smaller than the holes and passes through; the mustard seeds (2 mm) are bigger and stay on the sieve. (c) 300 g = 3,00,000 mg, and 3,00,000 / 5 = 60,000 seeds. (d) A poor suggestion. Handpicking is convenient only when the particles to be removed are few and easy to pick; about 60,000 tiny seeds spread through 2 kg of sooji would take far too long. Sieving separates them in a few minutes because the two differ in size.
s: (a) Magnet, because the iron pins are magnetic and the rest is not
(b) Sooji passes through the 1 mm holes; mustard seeds stay on the sieve
(c) About 60,000 seeds
(d) Rejects handpicking: 60,000 seeds are not few; sieving by size is far quicker

questions.q:
A dry mixture contains whole moong, fine sand, iron filings about as fine as the sand, and a few small stones about the same size as the moong. Rohit writes this plan:
Step 1: Add water to the mixture and filter it.
Step 2: Evaporate the filtrate to get the sand back.
Step 3: Move a magnet through the moong to pull out the stones.
Step 4: Sieve the sand to remove the iron filings.
(a) to (d): For each of Steps 1 to 4, say what is wrong with it. (e) Write a correct plan in the right order.
questions.a: (a) Step 1: none of the four components dissolves in water, so all of them stay together on the filter as residue; nothing is separated. (b) Step 2: the sand is insoluble and is not in the filtrate, so evaporating the filtrate gives no sand; evaporation gets back only a solid dissolved in a liquid. (c) Step 3: stones are not magnetic, so the magnet cannot pull them out. (d) Step 4: the iron filings are about the same size as the sand grains, so they pass through the sieve with the sand; sieving needs a difference in size. (e) First move a magnet through the dry mixture to remove the iron filings; then sieve with holes smaller than the moong but bigger than the sand grains, so the sand passes; then handpick the few stones from the moong, using their difference in colour and shape.
s: (a) Step 1 fails: nothing dissolves, so everything stays together as residue
(b) Step 2 fails: sand is not dissolved, so it is not in the filtrate
(c) Step 3 fails: stones are not magnetic
(d) Step 4 fails: filings are the same size as the sand and pass through with it
(e) Correct order: magnet for filings, sieve for sand, handpick the stones
